title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — aeterna most proper; includes corporal
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. But I will answer that when it is a matter of God's forum no death is more properly called death than eternal death: from which if corporal death is separated, it ought no longer even to be called death, by Christ himself as author: For the law does not threaten it except insofar as it is the loss of all goods of this life. But it is not a loss when better things succeed into their place. Add that eternal death includes the corporal, that is, the privation of this life, so that the law could not threaten that without at the same time threatening this.
pass_b_english: PLAC. I answer: before God's court no death is more properly called death than eternal death. If you split bodily death off from it, even that no longer deserves the name 'death,' by Christ's own teaching. The law threatens eternal death only as the loss of all this life's goods—and that is no loss when better goods take their place. Add that eternal death includes the bodily—the loss of this life—so the law could not threaten the one without also threatening the other.
source_text: PLAC. Ego vero respondebo, cum de foro Dei agitur nullam magis proprie mortem dici quam aeternam: a qua si corporalis sejungitur, ne mors quidem amplius vocari debet ipso Christo autore: Eam enim non comminatur lex, nisi quatenus est jactura omnium huius vitae bonorum. Jactura autem non est, cum in eorum locum succedunt meliora. Adde quod mors aeterna corporalem includit, id est, huius vitae privationem, ut illam: comminari lex non potuerit, quin istam simul comminaretur.
